{{Short description|Algorithm for finding roots of a function}}
{{More footnotes|date=February 2020}}
'''Muller's method''' is a [[root-finding algorithm]], a [[numerical analysis|numerical]] method for solving equations of the form {{math|1=''f''(''x'') = 0}}. It was first presented by [[David E. Muller]] in 1956.

[[File:Muller's method animation.gif|thumb|right|upright=1.25|
Animation illustrating Muller's method applied to the function {{math|1=''f''(''x'') = cos(''x'') − ''x''}}.
At each iteration, a parabola interpolating three points is constructed, and one of its
roots is used to generate the next approximation.]]

Muller's method proceeds according to a third-order [[recurrence relation]] similar to the second-order recurrence relation of the [[secant method]]. Whereas the secant method proceeds by constructing a line through two points on the graph of {{mvar|f}} corresponding to the last two iterative approximations and then uses the line's root as the next approximation at every iteration, by contrast, Muller's method uses three points corresponding to the last three iterative approximations, constructs a [[parabola]] through these three points, and then uses a root of the parabola as the next approximation at every iteration.

==Derivation==

Muller's method uses three initial approximations of the root, <math>x_{0}, x_{1}</math> and {{tmath|x_{2} }}, and determines the next approximation <math>x_{3}</math> by considering the intersection of the x-axis with the parabola through {{tmath|(x_{0}, f(x_{0}))}}, <math>(x_{1}, f(x_{1}))</math> and {{tmath|(x_{2}, f(x_{2}))}}.

Consider the quadratic polynomial
<math display="block"> P(x) = a(x - x_{2})^2 + b(x - x_{2}) + c,</math>

that passes through {{tmath|(x_{0}, f(x_{0}))}}, <math>(x_{1}, f(x_{1}))</math> and {{tmath|(x_{2}, f(x_{2}))}}. To simplify notation, define the differences

<math display="block">
h_{0} = x_{1} - x_{0}, \quad h_{1} = x_{2} - x_{1}
</math>

and
<math display="block">
\delta_{0} = \frac{f(x_{1}) - f(x_{0})}{h_{0}}, \quad
\delta_{1} = \frac{f(x_{2}) - f(x_{1})}{h_{1}}.
</math>

Substituting each of the three points {{tmath|(x_{0}, f(x_{0}))}}, <math>(x_{1}, f(x_{1}))</math> and <math>(x_{2}, f(x_{2}))</math> into <math>P(x)</math> and solving simultaneously for <math>a, b</math> and <math>c</math> gives

<math display="block">
a = \frac{\delta_{1} - \delta_{0}}{h_{1} + h_{0}}, \quad b = ah_{1} + \delta_{1}, \quad c = f(x_{2}).
</math>

The [[quadratic formula]] is then applied to <math>P(x)</math> to determine <math>x_{3}</math> as

<math display="block">
x_{3} - x_{2} = \frac{-2c}{b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}.
</math>

The sign preceding the radical term is chosen to match the sign of <math>b</math> to ensure the next iterate is closest to {{tmath|x_{2} }}, giving

<math display="block">
x_{3} = x_{2} - \frac{2c}{b + \operatorname{sign}(b)\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}.
</math>

Once <math>x_{3}</math> is determined, the process is repeated. Note that due to the radical expression in the denominator, iterates can be [[Complex number|complex]] even when the previous iterates are all real. This is in contrast with other root-finding algorithms like the [[secant method]], [[Sidi's generalized secant method]] or [[Newton's method]], whose iterates will remain real if one starts with real numbers. Having complex iterates can be an advantage (if one is looking for complex roots) or a disadvantage (if it is known that all roots are real), depending on the problem.

The method can easily be adopted for scenarios, such as collision detection, where not the closest root is of interest, but the smaller one by replacing <math>\operatorname{sign}(b)</math> with <math>\operatorname{sign}(-a)</math>:
<math display="block">
x_{3} = x_{2} - \frac{2c}{b - \operatorname{sign}(a)\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}.
</math>

== Algorithm ==
The following [[pseudocode]] describes Muller's method for approximating a root of the equation {{math|1=''f''(''x'') = 0}}. It returns an estimate <math>x_{3}</math> that satisfies {{tmath|{{!}}x_{3} - x_{2}{{!}} < \varepsilon}}, where <math>\varepsilon</math> is a user-specified tolerance.

 '''input:''' function {{mvar|f}}, initial approximations {{math|''x0''}}, {{math|''x1''}}, {{math|''x2''}}, tolerance {{mvar|ε}}, maximum iterations {{math|''Nmax''}}
 '''for''' ''n'' = 0 to ''Nmax'' '''do'''
    ''h0'' ← ''x1'' − ''x0''
    ''h1'' ← ''x2'' − ''x1''
    ''δ0'' ← (''f''(''x1'') − ''f''(''x0'')) / ''h0''
    ''δ1'' ← (''f''(''x2'') − ''f''(''x1'')) / ''h1''
    ''a'' ← (''δ1'' − ''δ0'') / (''h1'' + ''h0'')
    ''b'' ← ''a''·''h1'' + ''δ1''
    ''c'' ← ''f''(''x2'')
    '''if''' ''b'' ≥ 0 '''then'''
        ''denominator'' ← ''b'' + sqrt(''b''² − 4·''a''·''c'')
    '''else'''
        ''denominator'' ← b − sqrt(''b''² − 4·''a''·''c'')
    '''end if'''
    ''x3'' ← ''x2'' − 2·''c'' / ''denominator''
    '''if''' |''x3'' − ''x2''| < ''ε'' '''then'''
        '''return''' ''x3''
    '''end if'''
    ''x0'' ← ''x1''
    ''x1'' ← ''x2''
    ''x2'' ← ''x3''
 '''end for'''
 '''return''' ''x3''

Suppose we seek a solution of the polynomial
<math display="block">f(x) = -x^3 - x + 7 \,.</math>

Applying Muller's method with initial guesses {{tmath|1=x_{0}=1}}, <math>x_{1}=2</math> and <math>x_{2}=3</math> and a tolerance of <math>10^{-9}</math> gives the following approximations:

==Speed of convergence==
Suppose the real-valued function <math>f(x)</math> has a root at {{tmath|1=x=\alpha}}. Let
<math display="block">
e_{n} = x_{n} - \alpha
</math>
denote the error at the {{tmath|n}}-th iteration of Muller's method. By definition, we have
<math display="block">
e_{n+1} = K  e_{n}^{p}
</math>
where <math>p</math> is the [[order of convergence]] and <math>K</math> is an asymptotic constant. Therefore,
<math display="block">
e_{n} = K  e_{n-1}^{p}
</math>
and
<math display="block">
e_{n-1} = K  e_{n-2}^{p}
</math>
which gives
<math display="block">
e_{n-1} \sim e_{n}^{1/p}
</math>
and
<math display="block">
e_{n-2} \sim e_{n}^{1/p^2}.
</math>
Near the root {{tmath|1=x=\alpha}}, [[Taylor's theorem]] gives
<math display="block">
f(x) = f'(\alpha)(x - \alpha) + \frac{f''(\alpha)}{2}(x - \alpha)^{2} + R(x)
</math>
where <math>R(x)</math> is the remainder term, defined as
<math display="block">
R(x) = \frac{f'''(\xi)}{6}(x - \alpha)^{3}
</math>
for some <math>\xi</math> between <math>x</math> and {{tmath|\alpha}}. Using the three consecutive iterates of Mullers method, {{tmath|1=x=x_{n} }}, <math>x=x_{n-1}</math> and <math>x=x_{n-2}</math> evaluated at the root gives

<math display="block">
R(\alpha) = O(e_{n}e_{n-1}e_{n-2})
</math>
or
<math display="block">
e_{n+1} = O(e_{n}e_{n-1}e_{n-2})
</math>
since the next iterate is obtained by setting the interpolating quadratic to zero. Asymptotically,
<math display="block">
e_{n+1} = Ke_{n}e_{n-1}e_{n-2}.
</math>
Using
<math display="block">
e_{n-1} \sim e_{n}^{1/p}
</math>
and
<math display="block">
e_{n-2} \sim e_{n}^{1/p^2}
</math>
gives
<math display="block">
e_{n+1} = K e_{n}^{1 + \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p^2}}.
</math>

By definition,
<math display="block">
e_{n+1} = K e_{n}^{p}
</math>
so equating exponents gives
<math display="block">
p = 1 + \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p^2}
</math>
which can be rearranged to give

<math display="block">
p^{3} - p^{2} - p - 1 = 0.
</math>

Solving this equation gives {{tmath|p \approx 1.839}}, so the order of convergence of Muller's method is exactly the [[tribonacci constant]]. This can be compared with approximately 1.618, exactly the [[golden ratio]], for the [[secant method]] and with exactly 2 for [[Newton's method]]. So, the secant method makes less progress per iteration than Muller's method and Newton's method makes more progress.

More precisely, if <math>\alpha</math> denotes a single root of <math>f(x)</math> and <math>f'(\alpha) \neq 0</math> and <math>f(x)</math> is three times continuously differentiable, if the initial guesses {{tmath|x_{0} }}, <math>x_{1}</math> and <math>x_{2}</math> are taken sufficiently close to {{tmath|\alpha}}, then the iterates satisfy
<math display="block">
\lim_{k\to\infty} \frac{|x_k-\alpha|}{|x_{k-1}-\alpha|^\mu} = \left| \frac{f'''(\alpha)}{6f'(\alpha)} \right|^{(\mu-1)/2}
</math>

where <math>\mu \approx 1.84</math> is the positive solution of {{tmath|1=x^3 - x^2 - x - 1 = 0}}, the defining equation for the tribonacci constant.

==Generalizations and related methods==

Muller's method fits a parabola, i.e. a second-order [[polynomial]], to the last three obtained points {{math|''f''(''x''<sub>''k''−1</sub>)}}, {{math|''f''(''x''<sub>''k''−2</sub>)}} and {{math|''f''(''x''<sub>''k''−3</sub>)}} in each iteration. One can generalize this and fit a polynomial {{math|''p''<sub>''k'',''m''</sub>(''x'')}} of [[Degree of a polynomial|degree]] {{mvar|m}} to the last {{math|''m''+1}} points in the {{mvar|k}}-th iteration. Our parabola {{math|''y''<sub>''k''</sub>}} is written as {{math|''p''<sub>''k'',2</sub>}} in this notation. The degree {{mvar|m}} must be 1 or larger. The next approximation {{math|''x''<sub>''k''</sub>}} is now one of the roots of the {{math|''p''<sub>''k'',''m''</sub>}}, i.e. one of the solutions of {{math|1=''p''<sub>''k'',''m''</sub>(''x'') = 0}}. Taking {{math|1=''m'' = 1}} we obtain the secant method whereas {{math|1=''m'' = 2}} gives Muller's method.

Muller calculated that the sequence {{math|{{mset|''x''<sub>''k''</sub>}}}} generated this way converges to the root ξ with an order {{math|''μ''<sub>''m''</sub>}} where {{math|''μ''<sub>''m''</sub>}} is the positive solution of {{tmath|1=x^{m+1} - x^m - x^{m-1} - \dots - x - 1 = 0}}.

As {{mvar|m}} approaches infinity the positive solution for the equation approaches 2. The method is much more difficult though for {{math|''m'' > 2}} than it is for {{math|1=''m'' = 1}} or {{math|1=''m'' = 2}} because it is much harder to determine the roots of a polynomial of degree 3 or higher. Another problem is that there seems no prescription of which of the roots of {{math|''p''<sub>''k'',''m''</sub>}} to pick as the next approximation {{math|''x''<sub>''k''</sub>}} for {{math|''m'' > 2}}.

These difficulties are overcome by [[Sidi's generalized secant method]] which also employs the polynomial {{math|''p''<sub>''k'',''m''</sub>}}. Instead of trying to solve {{math|1=''p''<sub>''k'',''m''</sub>(''x'') = 0}}, the next approximation {{math|''x''<sub>''k''</sub>}} is calculated with the aid of the derivative of {{math|''p''<sub>''k'',''m''</sub>}} at {{math|''x''<sub>''k''−1</sub>}} in this method.
